text: This section reviews the 44 primary studies that were shortlisted in Section 2.3.8. The review is organised by the six key requirements of Section 2.2, so that Sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.6 correspond to Req 1 to Req 6 respectively. Each subsection reviews the primary studies that were assigned to that stream, states their issues and limitations with respect to the requirement in question, and ends with a table that summarises the studies and records their commitment to all six requirements, where √ denotes that the requirement is satisfied, ~ denotes that it is partially satisfied and × denotes that it is not satisfied, as coded from the full texts using the codebook described in Section 2.3. It should be noted that each study is assigned to one stream only, according to the requirement to which its main contribution relates; a study assigned to one stream may nevertheless be discussed briefly in another subsection when its coding is relevant to that requirement. The background surveys and position papers [1]–[34] are used only for context and do not appear in the tables, which list the 44 primary studies only.

title: Consent Representation and Blockchain-Based Consent Governance

text: This section reviews the twelve studies whose main contribution is the representation and governance of patient consent, in most cases on a blockchain. Req 1 requires that consent is represented as a structured object whose components, namely the participating identities, the authority requirements, the permitted purpose and data scope, the temporal validity, the jurisdiction and the supporting evidence, can be evaluated at the time of each request. Earlier consent-management research represented consent as a permission indicating whether a party may perform an operation, and dynamic consent and consent receipts added the possibility of changing preferences over time and of retaining evidence of how consent was obtained [13, 10]. The question examined in this stream is whether the reviewed systems go beyond a stored consent record and make the consent itself an object that the access decision evaluates. The full-text coding shows that all twelve studies were graded Partial on Req 1 and that none was graded Yes. In this context, three situations recur: consent that is represented but absent from the decision, consent that is present in the decision but reduced to a boolean flag, and consent that is held in a registry whose status is displayed or queried but never enforced.

The first group represents consent as a permission flag on a ledger. Akter and Sanam [36] implement a Hyperledger Fabric framework in which a stored consent record with an Active status is checked as the first conjunct of the access decision, followed by a role check, with a named deny path (ConsentNotGranted). The consent object is, however, a per-record boolean: it names no grantee, no purpose, no temporal bounds and no lifecycle operation, since no grant, revoke, withdraw or expiry operation is defined anywhere in the paper. The evaluation times the decision path (below 350 ms) but reports no denial, although three deny-log types are designed. Prashanth et al. [60] deploy a Solidity contract in which the decision is the conjunction of an owner whitelist and a per-(user, record) patient grant, with grantAccess and revokeAccess operations and events; the post-revocation denial is never demonstrated, no roles, purposes or temporal terms are evaluated, and the results consist of two gas figures and interface screenshots. Dhanraj et al. [42] combine federated learning with a Ganache testnet in which consent exists only as a Consent Logging contract call with a measured gas cost, and EHR Access Authorization exists only as a function name; no consent object, no authorisation predicate, no deny path and no identity mechanism are described, and the four contract operations are timed but never exercised as decisions. Sawant and Gomes [65] present FabricMedChain, a Fabric consortium with chaincode-enforced role-based access control and Caliper benchmarking; consent is mentioned repeatedly in the prose, yet the formal decision in Eq. (5) and the enforcement algorithm evaluate role-permission membership only, so consent is unrepresented in the decision despite the claims. The section titled formal security analysis contains a threat model and a simulated adversarial campaign but no formal method, and the broadest measurement campaign in the corpus never verifies the authorisation function it formalises.

The second group binds consent to cryptographic operations. Zhang et al. [78] combine a consortium Ethereum network with ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption for cross-enterprise document sharing; the access policy is embedded once, at encryption time, by the hospital server from two fixed templates, and it is evaluated cryptographically at each decryption. The patient does not author the policy, no purpose term exists, the time-aware property is an integer date comparison against an attribute fixed in the key at key generation, so that an in-window key decrypts indefinitely after expiry, and revocation consists of asking the server to delete a key it holds. Teeda and Subba Rao [70] propose a patient-centric scheme with identity-based proxy re-encryption in which consent is a per-request triple of a ciphertext share, a re-encryption key and a session time; there is no consent object, no state and no record, nothing is implemented, no revocation exists, and the printed correctness derivation is algebraically inconsistent. Ranaweera et al. [68] implement a zero-knowledge-proof login, homomorphic encryption for research outsourcing and an Ethereum consent workflow; the insurance access purpose is a free-text comment that the patient reads and approves manually, the granular time-scoped role-based access layer is named but not specified, and although a manual revocation followed by a refused re-access is demonstrated, the claimed automatic expiry is untested and its enforcement locus is unspecified.

The third group consists of deployed platforms and research infrastructures. Soohoo et al. [67] describe the authentication and authorisation module of the iAgree portal, deployed across three United States health systems, with OAuth2, SMART on FHIR and one-time-password identity that was tested with matched and unmatched accounts. Consent is a preference matrix of data category by recipient type whose enforcement is outside the scope of the paper, a single patient decides, the one-hour window is a session token rather than a consent validity period, and revocation is append-only and untested. Tremper et al. [72] report ten years of the Mainzelliste pseudonymisation and consent-management service, an open-source production tool with modular FHIR consent directives scoped by use type and an automated consent-check capability. The paper specifies no check semantics, no term list and no allow or deny protocol; consent withdrawal is implemented at the registry level through an API delete, with no downstream enforcement shown; the reason for each request is captured for audit but not adjudicated; and the security evidence is an independent penetration test and a secure development process rather than a formal analysis. Wagner et al. [74] integrate the gICS consent service, E-PIX identity management and pseudonymisation into a REDCap electronic data capture system; consent is held as modular policies with consented and not-consented states that are displayed to study personnel and queried through an interface, but nothing in the system makes an access decision depend on that state, so that data-use governance remains organisational.

The fourth group is conceptual. Bhalerao [39] proposes a design-only blueprint combining symmetric encryption, attribute-based encryption and smart contracts for consent and policy checking; no code, deployment or dataset exists, the results are projected, formal verification is deferred to future work, and the paper's own gap analysis concedes that real-time revocation mechanisms remain underdeveloped. Chockalingam et al. [41] describe a dynamic-consent framework for cognitive digital twins with a context-aware decision engine that outputs grant, prompt or deny and escalates to a human; the engine has named inputs and example rules but no rule language, algorithm or enforcement, purpose enters only as a prompt to the user and not as an evaluated term, caregivers are recipients rather than co-authorisers, and the framework is explicitly unimplemented. It should be noted that this study unifies dynamic consent, trust and context in one design with the broadest vocabulary in the stream, while providing neither assurance nor evidence.

Taken together, the studies in this stream show that the representation of consent and the evaluation of consent have largely been developed apart. Where consent enters the access decision, it enters as a boolean [36, 60]; where the consent object is rich, as in the FHIR-based directives of Mainzelliste [72] and gICS [74], the evaluation semantics are unspecified or enforcement is left to the organisation; and where consent is bound to cryptography [78, 70], the conditions are fixed at encryption or key-issuance time and cannot be re-evaluated at the time of the request. In addition, none of the twelve studies verifies its own authorisation decisions: those that are implemented report latency, gas or throughput without a single allow or deny correctness case, and Req 6 is graded No for ten of them. No study in this stream involves more than one authorising party, and Req 3 is graded No for all twelve. The closest single-party analogues of the consent object C = (I, A, P, T, L, E) required by the proposed framework are found not here but in Section 2.4.2, in the on-chain consent object of Phuyal et al. [58] and the consent token of Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66], and in the patient-driven policy of Al Amin et al. [38] in Section 2.4.3. Therefore, Req 1 is partially addressed throughout this stream, but consent as an object that is evaluated on every request against identity, authority, purpose, scope, time and jurisdiction is not provided by any of the reviewed consent-governance systems. Table 3 presents a summary of the studies in this stream and their commitment to the key requirements.

rows: A Hyperledger Fabric framework with Go chaincode and IPFS storage in which a stored consent record with an Active status is checked as the first conjunct of the decision, followed by role-based authorisation, with a named ConsentNotGranted deny path; a simulated prototype reports sub-350 ms access validation.

Consent is a per-record boolean with no grantee, purpose, temporal bounds or lifecycle operations (no grant, revoke, withdraw or expiry defined); roles are self-selected at login; three deny-log types are designed but no denial is reported; no threat model or formal content; no dataset or code release.

A design-only blueprint for cloud medical records combining AES-256-GCM, SHA-256 and CP-ABE with smart contracts for consent and policy checking; the decision flow validates attributes (role, department, clearance) against a policy before granting or denying and logging.

Nothing is implemented and the reported results are projected estimates; no consent object structure, no multi-party approval (the key ceremony is genesis bootstrapping), one clause on time-based restrictions, revocation only as a design mention; formal verification is explicitly future work.

A conceptual dynamic-consent framework for cognitive digital twins with a context-aware engine whose inputs include role, device, network, environment, time and human factors, and whose outputs are grant, prompt or deny with escalation; consent history and real-time revocation are narrated.

Self-declared conceptual with no implementation, simulation or evaluation; no rule language, algorithm or enforcement; purpose is a prompt to the user, not an engine input; caregivers are recipients, not co-authorisers; trust scores are named without any model; no security analysis of any kind.

A federated-learning diagnosis pipeline (TensorFlow Federated, three hospital nodes) anchored to a Ganache Ethereum testnet with four Solidity operations, including Consent Logging and EHR Access Authorization, whose gas and latency are measured on the UCI heart-disease dataset.

Consent is reduced to a logged event with a gas cost; no consent object, authorisation predicate, deny path or identity mechanism is described; the contract operations are timed but never exercised as decisions; no revocation or expiry; no security analysis; the hospital nodes are training parties, not authorisers.

A Solidity contract deployed in Remix for blockchain-based access management in which the decision is the conjunction of an owner whitelist and a per-(user, record) patient grant, with grantAccess and revokeAccess operations and on-chain events; deployment gas and interface panels are reported.

The consent is a boolean grant without roles, purpose, context or temporal terms; post-revocation denial is never demonstrated; wallet-address identity without credentials; no threat model or formal content; abstract-level benchmarking claims have no corresponding body evidence; no dataset, tests or code.

FabricMedChain, a Hyperledger Fabric v2.4 consortium with chaincode-enforced role-based access control, attribute-based certificates, break-glass override tokens and a DPoS overlay, benchmarked with Caliper on MIMIC-III-derived workloads including fault injection and six simulated attack classes.

Consent is mentioned throughout but is absent from the decision function Eq. (5), which evaluates role-permission membership only; no purpose or scope; the formal security analysis is a threat model and simulated attacks without formal methods; the extensive measurement campaign verifies no allow or deny decision; abstract figures contradict the body.

The authentication and authorisation module of the iAgree patient-controlled data-sharing portal, deployed at three health systems, with OAuth2, SMART on FHIR and one-time-password identity, a patient preference matrix of data category by recipient type, and a permissioned Ethereum audit contract.

A single patient decides and multi-institution is not multi-party; authorisation is OAuth2 delegation with no separate authority evidence for researchers; enforcement of the preference matrix is out of scope; the one-hour window is a session token, not consent validity; revocation is append-only and untested; no formal methods; functional tests only.

A web application with a Circom/Plonk zero-knowledge-proof wallet login, BFV homomorphic encryption for research outsourcing, an Ethereum consent workflow for insurance access requests, and a manual single-click revocation that was shown to refuse subsequent re-access.

The zero-knowledge proof authenticates wallet ownership only; the access reason is free text read by the patient, not an evaluated purpose; the time-scoped role layer is named without schema or algorithm; automatic expiry is claimed but untested with an unspecified locus; single-locus consent; no formal analysis, measurements, dataset or code.

A patient-centric electronic health record scheme in which the record ciphertext is split between the chain and the patient wallet, and each access is authorised by the patient supplying a share, an identity-based proxy re-encryption key and a user-defined session time to a smart contract.

No implementation, simulation or measurement of any kind; consent is a per-request cryptographic act with no object, state or record; no policy, purpose, role or scope; no revocation; the session expiry is unenforceable after delivery because the doctor decrypts with a permanent key; the printed correctness derivation is defective.

Mainzelliste, an open-source pseudonymisation, record-linkage and consent-management service in production since 2015, with multi-tenant role-based access control, per-request token validation, modular FHIR consent directives scoped by use type, an automated consent-check capability and registry-level consent withdrawal.

The consent-check semantics, term list and allow or deny protocol are not specified in the paper; withdrawal is a registry operation whose downstream enforcement is not shown; no temporal validity; the secure multi-party computation parties perform record linkage, not authorisation; security evidence is a penetration test without formal analysis; no consent decision is verified.

Integration of the gICS consent service, E-PIX identity management and a pseudonymisation dispatcher into the REDCap electronic data capture system, released as an open-source module, in which modular consent policies carry consented or not-consented states that study personnel can view and query.

Consent state is displayed and queried but no access decision depends on it, so enforcement remains organisational; project-scoped roles without case-specific authority; the trusted third party is a pseudonymisation unit, not an authoriser; no temporal terms; withdrawal effect on downstream data not shown; no threat model; functional description only.

A cross-enterprise document-sharing and dynamic-consent framework on a consortium Ethereum network with a smart-contract registry, IPFS storage and ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption in which a hospital server embeds one of two fixed access policies at encryption time and the patient issues decryption keys.

The patient does not author the policy and no purpose term exists; the time-aware property compares a date fixed in the key at issuance, so an in-window key decrypts after expiry; revocation is honest-server key deletion and the custodial key is irrevocable; no credentials; no formal analysis; performance measured with no allow or deny or attack test.

text: This section reviews the five studies whose main contribution is the decentralised verification of the participants in a consent decision. Req 2 requires that the patient, the guardians, the healthcare professional and the institution can be identified without a single central identity provider, and that establishing who a participant is (identity) is treated separately from establishing what that participant may do (authority), each with its own evidence. Decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials provide the first capability [20, 33, 4, 16], and the reviewed studies apply them, or national equivalents, to healthcare data exchange. It should be noted that the coding distinguishes T1 (identity established by DID, VC, PKI or certificate) from T2 (case-specific authority verified separately from authentication). Across the 44 primary studies, T2 was graded Yes in only 10 studies and Partial in 34; that is, in more than three quarters of the corpus a verified identity, a platform role or an administratively assigned attribute stands in for authority over a particular patient's data.

Phuyal et al. [58] present the most integrated system in the corpus, a simulated Norwegian cross-institution exchange in which patients and professionals hold EUDI-compatible wallets with W3C decentralised identifiers and verifiable credentials, consent is an executable on-chain object carrying the patient identifier, the requester identifier, the data scope and an expiry together with an ACTIVE or REVOKED state on a Hyperledger Besu ledger, and access proofs are generated with Groth16 circuits. Identity verification checks the issuer registry, the signature and the credential expiry, and, importantly for Req 2, a licensing-body credential asserts the professional's role, specialisation and scope of practice, which the system verifies separately from authentication. This is the strongest Req 2 evidence in the corpus. Revocation is enforced at run time in 1.45 seconds and subsequent access returns an error, and allow and deny cases are tested over 100 runs per workflow. The limitations are equally precise: a single patient grants a bilateral data-sharing agreement and there is no multi-party approval, the expiry field is stored on the ledger but the access algorithm checks only state and proof, purpose exists only at the user-interface level, and there is no threat model, formal verification or adversarial test. The companion architecture of Phuyal et al. [59] extends the design to secondary use with a FHIR Consent resource carrying purpose, scope, actors and validity period, and specifies validation of these constraints at decision time; however, the authors state that nothing is implemented or evaluated, so every dimension is capped at Partial, and the proxy or guardian delegation mentioned as an option is substitution rather than joint approval.

Ferreira et al. [45] integrate a permissioned ledger with a Model Context Protocol gateway over FHIR servers so that every entity holds a decentralised identifier, the requester's credential is verified at the consent check, and a single authorisation call conjoins the subject, the purpose, the scope and the time over the current consent state, with on-chain revocation lists invalidating cached grants. This is the widest designed predicate in the corpus. Nevertheless, case-specific authority reduces to the credential plus the consent state without separate authority evidence, the guardians named in the paper are a social key-recovery mechanism rather than co-authorisers, the contract interfaces are referenced but not shown, no code is released, the quantitative results are captioned as illustrative, and no allow or deny correctness matrix or attack test is reported. Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66] propose a self-sovereign identity and consent framework in which the consent token carries the patient identifier, a role, a scope with permissions, a validity interval and a three-state lifecycle, and the decision conjoins a zero-knowledge proof of an issuer-signed provider credential with scope validity, temporal validity and lifecycle state. The token is the closest single-party structural analogue of the consent object required by the proposed framework, but the patient identifier is a self-generated key pair without proofing, the role-to-token match is described in prose rather than in the formal predicate, the issuer trust root is unspecified, the reported stack is internally inconsistent (Hyperledger Fabric with Solidity contracts, PBFT and gas in gwei), and no denial after revocation or expiry is tested.

Tseng et al. [73] present EMR-Chain, an open-source decentralised medical record exchange that combines an Ethereum identity chain with a Hyperledger Fabric record chain. The identifier is a government-endorsed hashed national identity bound to a wallet, which the authors call a DID although it is not a W3C decentralised identifier; professional identities are X.509 certificates issued by the ministry certificate authority, and roles are granted by the health authority, so that authority is verified separately from authentication. The system is benchmarked against national exchange statistics and the code is public. Its limitations with respect to the later requirements are that the patient and requester co-signature on a request is bilateral authentication rather than independent approval, purpose is logged in the transaction record but never evaluated, scope is at the hospital level, the token expiry enforced at the validator is a session bound rather than a consent validity window, revocation of the access list does not invalidate tokens already issued, and the security discussion is narrative.

In summary, identity is the strongest dimension of this stream, with T1 graded Yes in four of the five studies, but authority verified with its own evidence is found only in Phuyal et al. [58] through licensing-body credentials and in Tseng et al. [73] through authority-issued roles. The remaining eight Yes gradings for T2 in the corpus belong to other streams, and several of them do not use decentralised identifiers at all: Ekholm et al. [43] and Hagström et al. [47] verify legal guardianship against a national population register, Madine et al. [53] rely on a regulatory agency, and Punia et al. [61] bind roles, attributes and access tokens to their owners independently of the sender address. In addition, the studies of this stream that come closest to an evaluable consent object [58, 45, 66] are single-party designs, none of them is formally assured, and only Phuyal et al. [58] verify allow and deny outcomes. Therefore, the literature provides mature mechanisms for decentralised identity and increasingly for credential-based authority, but it does not yet combine separated identity and authority evidence with multi-party approval, policy evaluation and formal assurance in one decision. Table 4 presents a summary of the studies in this stream and their commitment to the key requirements.

Authority reduces to the credential plus consent state with no separate authority evidence; the guardians are key recovery, not co-authorisers; single patient issues consent; contract interfaces are referenced but not shown and no code is released; results are captioned illustrative; no allow or deny matrix or attack test; threat model only, no proof.

A simulated Norwegian cross-institution exchange with EUDI-compatible wallets, W3C DIDs and VCs, an executable on-chain consent object (patient DID, requester DID, scope, expiry, state) on Hyperledger Besu, Groth16 access proofs, licensing-body credentials asserting role and scope of practice, run-time revocation (1.45 s) and an openEHR to FHIR bridge; allow and deny outcomes tested over 100 runs.

A single patient grants a bilateral agreement with no multi-party approval; the expiry field is stored but the access algorithm checks only state and proof; purpose is at the user-interface level with no policy engine; no threat model, formal verification or adversarial test; simulation only with a node-count inconsistency.

A design-only architecture for dynamic and auditable consent in secondary use in which a FHIR Consent resource carrying purpose, scope, actors and validity period is anchored on an Ethereum-compatible ledger, requester credentials are validated in three steps at a gateway, and validation of purpose, scope and duration at decision time is specified.

Explicitly not implemented and not evaluated, so no dimension is enforced; proxy or guardian delegation is a substitution option rather than joint approval; revocation is specified but not implemented; the STRIDE-style threat table is declared non-exhaustive with no proof or verification; same author group as [58].

A self-sovereign identity and consent framework in which a patient-issued consent token carries identifier, role, scope and permissions, a validity interval and an ACTIVE, REVOKED or EXPIRED state, and the decision conjoins a ZoKrates zero-knowledge proof of an issuer-signed provider credential with scope, temporal and lifecycle validity; simulated on four peers with 100 to 10,000 synthetic records.

The patient DID is a self-generated key pair without proofing and the issuer trust root is unspecified; the role-to-token match is prose, not part of the formal predicate; no purpose of use; no denial after revocation or expiry is tested; the stack is internally inconsistent (Fabric with Solidity, PBFT, gas in gwei); one qualitative threat paragraph; author-assigned comparator scores.

EMR-Chain, an open-source decentralised record exchange combining an Ethereum identity chain, on which a government-endorsed hashed national identity is bound to a wallet, with a Hyperledger Fabric record chain using X.509 identities from the ministry certificate authority, health-authority-granted roles, a patient-adjustable per-hospital access list and JWT validation, benchmarked against national exchange statistics.

The identifier is not a W3C DID; the patient and requester co-signature is bilateral authentication, not independent approval; purpose is logged but never evaluated and scope is hospital-level; JWT expiry is a session bound rather than consent validity; access-list revocation does not invalidate issued tokens; narrative security discussion only.

text: This section reviews the eight studies whose main contribution involves the participation of more than one party in a consent or access decision. Req 3 requires that, where a single party cannot lawfully authorise access on its own, a predefined number of designated parties must each provide an independently verifiable approval, and that this threshold condition is represented within the consent object and can be checked by any party at a later time. An earlier version of this review, which was based on the background corpus [1]–[34], stated that multi-party joint authorisation of patient data access had not been realised in the literature. The full-text coding of the present corpus does not support that statement, and it is withdrawn. Across the 44 primary studies, T3 (at least two distinct independent participants must approve) was graded Yes in 6 studies, Partial in 4 and No in 34, and the coding panel ratified six distinct mechanism classes of multi-party authorisation. It should be noted that the coding applied a strict word-sense discipline: blockchain consensus, endorsement policies, multi-authority attribute-based encryption, secure multi-party computation parties, requester co-signatures and social key-recovery guardians were not counted as multi-party authorisation, because none of them adds an independent authoriser to the decision. The purpose of this section is therefore to state precisely which forms of multi-party authorisation exist and which form does not.

The first class is joint approval on a contingency path. Madine et al. [53] propose a fully decentralised multi-party consent scheme on Ethereum in which an access request on the incapacitated path requires the approvals of a regulatory agency and of at least the minimum of ceil(0.7g) and five guardians on the same request, and an emergency request requires the agency's approval together with a hospital admission confirmation. This is a genuine N-of-M condition over independent parties, and it is combined with expiry enforced inside the decision predicate, since stale attestations stop counting, and with explicit revocation of claims and removal of guardians. However, on the normal path a single patient key authorises access, so that joint approval is an availability fallback conditioned on the absence of the principal rather than a condition of every decision. In addition, the guardians hold no key shares: the decryption key is split between the patient and the regulatory agency, which can decrypt with its own shares, so the joint guarantee holds at the smart-contract layer only and the claim of full decentralisation is asserted rather than demonstrated. The paper contains no formal analysis, no dataset and no allow or deny correctness matrix. Abbasi et al. [35] present Nexa, a public-blockchain record system in which a Shamir (5, 3) threshold protects each record key; a clinical access combines the requester's own share with two automated oracle shares that are released on the basis of the current on-chain role, so there is a single authorisation locus and no human co-approval, the patient's share is not required, and the institutional multi-signature for bulk access is proposed but outside the prototype. The prototype is public and measured, but no authorisation decision is verified. A related design in Section 2.4.6, Maruthi and Singh [54], releases the key of an unconscious patient through a t-of-n threshold over patient-designated relatives under proxy re-encryption with indistinguishability proofs, but with no policy or temporal term.

The second class places the threshold on the institution side. Wu et al. [75] present Soteria, a clinical-trial data platform on Hyperledger Fabric with trusted-execution chaincode in which a (t, n) threshold signature runs over named investigators. What the threshold gates is asymmetric: the admission of a trial record to the ledger requires a majority of investigators, and the revocation of a consent requires the approval of half of them, whereas the consent grant itself is submitted unilaterally by the patient. Moreover, each investigator's vote consists of recomputing and confirming the hash of the message, so the threshold is a threshold of integrity verifiers rather than of authorisers, and the voters are institution-side investigators rather than parties acting for the patient. The fifth class is institutional custodian approval conjoined with a policy engine. Punia et al. [61] implement MedXBlock, a permissioned Ethereum access-control system in which an M-of-N multi-signature contract over registered doctors and administrators, for example two of three, governs high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, and in which an implemented hybrid attribute- and role-based policy engine evaluates a conjunctive grant predicate with deny-by-default over a stateful policy store. This is the only study in the corpus in which multi-party approval and an enforced policy predicate co-occur. Even so, the threshold is scoped, since ordinary access is token-only, it is defeasible, since a single emergency officer can bypass it, and it sits outside the grant predicate as a separate orchestration layer; the patient enters the predicate as a boolean consent attribute rather than as an authoriser; no purpose term exists; the assurance is a threat table and an asserted safety property; and the 100 measured transactions include no executed authorisation test.

The fourth class appoints witnesses. Tan et al. [69] propose a personal health record sharing scheme with multi-party pre-authorisation verification in which the patient fixes n verifiers and a threshold t, each verifier evaluates the patient-issued grant, its expiry and the revocation list before releasing its share of the decryption key, and without t shares no key and no plaintext exist. This is the first threshold in the corpus whose authorisers are appointed by the patient for the patient's own access decision, and expiry is checked at the point of approval. The joint approval is nevertheless a pre-delegated contingency mechanism for the case in which the patient is unable to act, the verifiers evaluate identity, grant, time and revocation but not purpose or data scope, since attribute-based policy is explicitly future work, only the secure multi-party computation layer of roughly 6500 lines is implemented while the identity, wallet and ledger layers are not, and the security argument is a STRIDE and LINDDUN enumeration with no proof over the authorisation protocol. The third class, reviewed in Section 2.4.6, is the consumer-side delegated threshold of Zhao and Su [50], in which l of d already-authorised clinicians jointly authorise an out-of-policy requester and the threshold gate carries an indistinguishability proof; the delegates are consumer-side rather than patient-side parties, and the scheme has no time, lifecycle or purpose term.

The sixth class is register-verified guardian co-consent at consent registration, and it is the only class found in deployed systems. Ekholm et al. [43] report the implementation of electronic informed consent in rare disease genomics on a commercial platform used by three genomic medicine centres in Sweden: the consent of a minor is valid only when all legal guardians, one or two, have signed, and guardianship is verified in real time against the national Population Register, with 61 paediatric trio consents obtained under this rule. This is a deployed n-of-n guardian condition with authority verified separately from the national electronic identity used for authentication, and it is the cleanest separation of identity and authority in the corpus. Its locus is, however, the registration of consent and not the access decision: the only decision-time touchpoint is an interface that answers whether a valid consent exists, without purpose, scope or time parameters, the platform is centralised, and the paper provides no formal or authorisation-correctness evidence. Hagström et al. [47] examine, in a retrospective comparative case study of the national patient portals of Sweden and Finland, how guardian proxy access to a minor's record is gated jointly by a healthcare professional's assessment of the minor's capacity and by the minor's own consent, with register-verified guardianship and age windows whose enforcement is demonstrated by the absence of use within blocked windows and by the consent of 95.8 per cent of capable minors to disclosure. This is a second deployed instance of collective, consent-gated proxy governance, but it is documentation-time governance in centralised national systems with no formal assurance. Finally, Al Amin et al. [38] represent informed consent as a patient-driven policy IC = (U, O, OP, CON), an evaluable object whose contextual conditions include time, date, day, location, network address and access frequency, and whose enforcement conjoins the patient's consent with organisational and regulatory policies. The only multi-party element is a two-of-two multi-signature wallet in the experimental harness in which every member must sign to store a consent; the members are not named, the mechanism gates registration rather than access, it is absent from the model, no purpose term exists, and the Goerli deployment reports no measured result or allow or deny case. The panel recorded it as a candidate class only.

The position of the literature with respect to Req 3 can therefore be stated precisely. What exists is multi-party authorisation in six forms: joint approval on a contingency path when the principal is absent [53, 69]; guardian or bilateral co-consent at the time of consent registration [43, 47, 38]; institution-side thresholds over record admission and consent revocation [75]; custodial M-of-N approval around, but not inside, a policy predicate [61]; a patient-appointed witness threshold welded to key release [69]; and threshold key custody or delegation among custodians, relatives or clinicians [35, 54, 50]. In this context, the sentence that multi-party authorisation does not exist in the literature is no longer defensible and is not made in this review. What does not exist in any of the 44 studies is a threshold predicate over the guardian set G with threshold N that is constitutive of the access decision, that is, one evaluated on every access request, in a decentralised exchange, as a conjunct of the same predicate that evaluates the policy conditions of purpose and data scope, the temporal validity and the jurisdiction of the consent object C, with allow and deny correctness evidence and formal assurance of the conjunction. The coding supports each element of this statement. Only Punia et al. [61] combine T3 = Yes with an enforced policy predicate, and there the threshold is outside the predicate, the patient is an attribute and purpose is absent. Every T3-positive study in this stream is graded No or Partial on Req 6, and the two T3-positive studies elsewhere that carry a proof [50, 54] prove the threshold gate or confidentiality in isolation, so that the broadest multi-party systems carry the weakest assurance. In addition, the deployed guardian mechanisms [43, 47] establish guardian authority through a state register, which is the attestation pattern against which the guardian credentials of the proposed framework must be compared. The threshold is over key custodians, not authorisers: a single authorisation locus with no human co-approval and the patient's share not required; the institutional multi-signature is outside the prototype; role-based only with no purpose, context or temporal term; no formal proof or tool; performance measured with no allow or deny or attack test; estimated competitor values.

Informed consent represented as a patient-driven policy IC = (U, O, OP, CON) with hash integrity and contextual conditions (time, date, day, location, network address, frequency) that an authorisation module conjoins with organisational and regulatory policies; a Solidity consent-management contract is deployed on the Goerli testnet.

The only multi-party element is a two-of-two multi-signature wallet in the test harness that gates consent registration, with unnamed members and no place in the model; no purpose term; lifecycle operations described but not specified; enforcement mechanisms explicitly not included; no measured result or allow or deny case; assumptions only, no security analysis.

Deployed electronic informed consent for rare disease genomics at three Swedish genomic medicine centres on a commercial platform: a minor's consent is valid only when all legal guardians sign, guardianship is verified in real time against the national Population Register, authentication uses the national electronic identity, and adoption is reported for 2,244 invited participants.

The guardian condition applies at consent registration, not to the access decision; the only decision-time touchpoint answers whether a valid consent exists, without purpose, scope or time; study-level broad consent with no policy; withdrawal effect not described; centralised research platform described in little technical detail; no formal or authorisation-correctness evidence; vendor conflict of interest declared.

A retrospective comparative case study of the Swedish and Finnish national patient portals in which guardian proxy access to a minor's record is gated jointly by a healthcare professional's capacity assessment and the minor's own consent, with register-verified guardianship and age windows whose enforcement is evidenced by no use within blocked windows and 95.8 per cent of capable minors consenting to disclosure.

The collective condition is documentation-time governance in centralised national systems rather than a decision-time predicate in a decentralised exchange; consent is not an evaluable object with its own scope or purpose; the study is observational and offers no security analysis or formal assurance.

A fully decentralised multi-party consent scheme on Ethereum in which incapacitated-path access requires regulatory-agency approvals and at least min(ceil(0.7g), 5) guardian approvals on one request, emergency access requires agency approval and hospital admission confirmation, attestation expiry is enforced inside the decision, and claims and guardians can be revoked; a testnet prototype with gas costs is reported.

On the normal path a single patient key authorises, so joint approval is a contingency fallback rather than a condition of every decision; guardians hold no key shares and the regulatory agency can decrypt alone, so the joint guarantee is contract-level only; no policy, purpose or data-category model; no formal analysis, dataset, attack test or allow or deny matrix.

MedXBlock, a permissioned Ethereum access-control system with an implemented hybrid attribute- and role-based policy engine evaluating a conjunctive deny-by-default predicate over a stateful policy store, an M-of-N multi-signature contract over registered doctors and administrators for high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, token expiry checked at access, and 100 instrumented transactions.

The threshold is institution-side, scoped to sensitive requests, bypassable by a single emergency officer and outside the grant predicate; patient consent is a boolean attribute, not an evaluable object with its own scope, validity or lifecycle; no purpose term; a threat table and an asserted safety property only; systems metrics with no executed authorisation, denial or attack test; gas figures internally inconsistent.

Personal health record sharing with multi-party pre-authorisation verification in which the patient appoints n verifiers and a threshold t; each verifier checks the patient-issued grant, its expiry and the revocation list before releasing a share of the decryption key, so that t validated shares are needed to obtain the record; the secure multi-party computation layer is implemented in Go on ten machines.

The joint approval is a pre-delegated contingency for an incapable patient; verifiers evaluate identity, grant, time and revocation but not purpose or data scope (attribute policy is future work); the identity, wallet, credential and ledger layers are not implemented; no authorisation test, no expired or revoked credential rejection test; STRIDE and LINDDUN enumeration with no proof over the protocol.

Soteria, a multi-site clinical-trial data platform on Hyperledger Fabric with trusted-execution chaincode in which a (t, n) threshold signature over named investigators gates the admission of trial records to the ledger and the revocation of a consent, consents carry enumerated states with start and end times and a study-number binding validated at an endpoint, and fourteen endpoints are timed on a managed deployment.

The consent grant is unilateral and the threshold governs record admission and revocation rather than the patient's access decision; each vote is a hash-integrity check by institution-side investigators; time is a stored attribute not shown to gate the decision; no policy engine; no theorem, proof or adversary model; performance only with borrowed latency figures and no correctness or attack evaluation.
